text: Jaguars' Bhayshul Tuten questionable for Thursday night vs. Ravens. Bhayshul Tuten is trending because the Jacksonville Jaguars listed the running back as questionable on the final injury report for Thursday night's Week 9 game at the Baltimore Ravens. He missed practice on Tuesday and Wednesday with a foot and ankle injury.. Bhayshul Tuten is a running back for the Jacksonville Jaguars. He has been dealing with injuries to his foot and ankle, and he did not practice on Tuesday or Wednesday this week. The Jaguars released their final injury report listing Tuten as questionable for the Week 9 game against the Baltimore Ravens. Head coach Liam Coen has said Tuten's status will likely be decided close to kickoff. Fantasy football players are also watching the situation, since Chris Rodriguez Jr. Would likely take on a bigger role if Tuten cannot play. The Jaguars defeated the Colts 42-7 the previous Sunday.. The Jaguars and Ravens play Thursday night in Baltimore, and Coen has said Tuten's status will be a game-time decision.

What happened to Dane Cook's brother? The $12 million theft. Dane Cook's half-brother and business manager, Darryl McCauley, stole at least $12 million from the comedian between 2004 and 2008. He and his wife, Erika, pleaded guilty in 2010 to theft, embezzlement and forgery. McCauley was sentenced to six years in prison and ordered to repay Cook, but after his release he disappeared without paying the money back.. "Funny Money: The Dane Cook Story," about the theft by his half-brother, arrives on Netflix in the U.S. On Nov. 6, 2026.. The theft is the subject of the documentary "Funny Money: The Dane Cook Story," which reaches Netflix in the U.S. On Nov. 6, 2026. Directed and written by Brett Harvey and narrated by Cook, it first premiered on Sept. 18 at the Aero Theatre in Los Angeles and went to digital stores on Sept. 29. It was commissioned by Canada's Super Channel under the title "Brace for Impact." It is a licensed film, not a Netflix original. The money vanished while Cook was one of the best-selling comedians of the 2000s. McCauley pulled out sums of $20,000, $50,000 and up to $100,000 at a time without Cook noticing, and hid cash in a safe and even wrapped in plastic inside pasta sauce containers. The scheme came to light after Cook hired a new business manager. Erika McCauley received two to three years. Cook believes the true loss may be higher than $12 million. As boys, both brothers wanted to be stand-up comics; McCauley became a corrections officer instead. Cook has called him "the devil that was my brother" and says he spent about a decade in therapy rebuilding his life.

Why are there two Dan Sullivans on the Alaska ballot?. Two Dan Sullivans are on Alaska's 2026 Senate ballot because a second man with the same name, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg, filed to run against Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan. The state tried to disqualify him, but Alaska's courts ordered his name kept on the ballot.. The Alaska Senate race between Mary Peltola and Senator Dan Sullivan is separated by a few hundred votes, and the second Sullivan's ballots could matter when ranked choices are counted on Nov. 18, 2026.. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. Is a retired teacher and former U.S. Forest Service employee. He filed as a Republican three days before the deadline, called himself a pragmatic centrist, and says he is no relation to the senator. Senator Sullivan called the bid a sham and dirty politics by Democrats. Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign and the state and national Democratic parties denied any link, though Alaska station KTUU found he had given small donations to Peltola's past campaigns, $100 in 2022 and $30 in 2024. The Division of Elections ruled on June 16, 2026 that his filing was not made in good faith and removed him. An Anchorage Superior Court judge reversed that on June 26, and the Alaska Supreme Court agreed on July 2. In the August top-four primary he won about 2.5%, enough to reach the November ballot. To limit confusion, the ballot lists him as "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr." with no party, and marks Dan S. Sullivan as the incumbent. He drew roughly 3,600 votes, about 1.7%, in the first count of the Nov. 3 general election, a race in which Peltola led the senator by only about 600 votes. Under ranked-choice rules he will be eliminated early, and his ballots will move to his voters' second choices in the count scheduled for Nov. 18.

Is Under Siege on Netflix a true story? The 1985 Bogotá siege. Yes. Netflix's "Under Siege" ("Palacio" in Spanish) is based on a real event: on Nov. 6, 1985, guerrillas of Colombia's M-19 movement seized the Palace of Justice in Bogotá and took about 300 hostages, including Supreme Court justices. The army's counterattack lasted about 28 hours, and more than 90 people were killed or went missing.. Netflix's Colombian drama "Under Siege" premieres on Nov. 6, 2026, the anniversary of the 1985 Palace of Justice siege it depicts.. The eight-part Colombian series premieres on Nov. 6, 2026, the 41st anniversary of the attack. It comes from Dynamo, the company behind "Narcos," with showrunner Natalia Santa, who also wrote Netflix's "One Hundred Years of Solitude." The cast includes Natalia Reyes, Carlos Manuel Vesga and Robinson Díaz. The story follows the hostages and soldiers, and then the families who spent two decades looking for relatives who never came home. Eleven Supreme Court magistrates died, among them Chief Justice Alfonso Reyes Echandía. At least 11 people, mostly workers from the building's cafeteria, were reported missing after the siege; the remains of some were identified only years later. A former hitman claimed Pablo Escobar paid the M-19 to destroy court records on extradition, but a 1986 government inquiry could not prove it. The disappearances led to decades of trials. Army Colonel Alfonso Plazas Vega was sentenced to 30 years in 2010 and later acquitted, while retired General Jesús Armando Arias Cabrales received 35 years. The M-19 laid down its arms in 1990 and became a political party.

What does designated for assignment mean? DFA in baseball. Designated for assignment, or DFA, means an MLB team has removed a player from its 40-man roster. The club then has up to seven days to trade him, put him on waivers, or release him. Waivers take 48 hours, so in practice a team has about five days to find a trade.. MLB teams clear 40-man roster spots ahead of the Nov. 17, 2026 Rule 5 protection deadline, and DFA moves pile up each November.. If another team claims the player on waivers, it takes over his contract. If no one claims him, his team can send him outright to the minors, though veterans with enough service time can refuse and become free agents. The player keeps being paid while he waits; that waiting period is often called "DFA limbo." The days between Christmas and New Year's Day do not count toward the seven. DFAs come in waves in November. Teams must add prospects to the 40-man roster by Nov. 17, 2026 to protect them from the Rule 5 draft, and the non-tender deadline follows on Nov. 20, so clubs clear spots by designating fringe players. A player picked up in the Rule 5 draft cannot be designated from the draft until 20 days before Opening Day, and a player just claimed off waivers cannot be designated again for at least 48 hours.

How is the MLB MVP voted? 30 writers, results Nov. 12. The MLB MVP is chosen by 30 members of the Baseball Writers' Association of America, two from each big league city, voting separately for the American and National League. Each lists 10 players; first place earns 14 points, then 9 down to 1. The 2026 MVPs will be announced Nov. 12.. MLB's 2026 award winners are announced Nov. 9-12, ending with the American and National League MVPs on Nov. 12.. The same writers' group picks the other main awards, with 30 voters each. The Cy Young ballot has five places worth 7, 4, 3, 2 and 1 points. Rookie of the Year and Manager of the Year ballots have three places worth 5, 3 and 1. Writers cannot split a place between two players, and AL cities vote only on AL awards, NL cities only on NL awards. Ballots are turned in before the postseason begins, so October heroics do not count. The 2026 schedule runs across one week on MLB Network: Rookie of the Year on Monday, Nov. 9, Manager of the Year on Nov. 10, Cy Young on Nov. 11 and MVP on Thursday, Nov. 12. Three finalists are named in advance for each award, and full vote totals are published after each announcement.

What does non-tender mean in baseball? MLB deadline is Nov. 20. To non-tender a player means an MLB team declines to offer him a contract for next season, so he becomes a free agent at once. It mostly happens to arbitration-eligible players whose next salary would be higher than the team wants to pay. The 2026 non-tender deadline is 4 p.m. Central on Nov. 20.. MLB's 2026 non-tender deadline falls on Nov. 20, less than two weeks before the labor agreement expires on Dec. 1.. Players with fewer than six years in the majors are still under team control. Each winter the team must "tender" them a contract by the deadline to keep them. Those eligible for salary arbitration can get large raises on their second, third and fourth trips through the process, so a club may let a useful but costly player go rather than risk an arbitrator's number. Teams also non-tender players with injury questions, or to free a spot on the 40-man roster. Non-tendered players skip waivers, can sign with any team, and sometimes return to their old club on a cheaper deal. This year the deadline carries extra weight. The labor agreement between owners and players expires at 11:59 p.m. Eastern on Dec. 1, 2026, and owners are widely expected to lock players out the next day. During a lockout, major league transactions freeze, so players cut on Nov. 20 would have only about 11 days to sign before the market could stop.

What is a qualifying offer in MLB? $23.15 million, decide by Nov. 17. A qualifying offer is a one-year contract that an MLB team can offer its own departing free agent. For the 2026-27 offseason it is worth $23.15 million, the average of the 125 highest salaries in baseball. Players have until 3 p.m. Central on Nov. 17 to accept; if one declines and signs elsewhere, his old team gets a draft pick.. MLB teams made qualifying offers to eight free agents after the 2026 World Series, and the players must decide by Nov. 17.. Eight players received the offer in early November 2026: Randy Arozarena (Mariners), Jake Bauers (Brewers), David Bednar (Yankees), Ryan Jeffers (Twins), Brandon Lowe (Pirates), Adrián Morejón (Padres), Trevor Rogers (Orioles) and Seiya Suzuki (Cubs). The amount is a record, up from $22.025 million a year earlier. A team can make the offer only if the player spent the whole season with it, and a player can receive one only once in his career. A player who accepts cannot be traded without his consent until June 15. The draft pick is what makes the offer matter. The pick the old team receives depends on its finances and the size of the new contract: a revenue-sharing team losing a player who signs for $50 million or more gets a pick after the first round, while a team that paid the luxury tax gets one only after the fourth round. The team that signs him pays a price too: a club over the luxury tax forfeits its second- and fifth-highest picks plus $1 million in international bonus money. Last offseason 13 players got the offer and 4 accepted it: Trent Grisham, Shota Imanaga, Gleyber Torres and Brandon Woodruff. This year the rule may be living its final winter: the labor contract that created it expires at 11:59 p.m. Eastern on Dec. 1, 2026, and a new deal could change or drop it.

What is the Rule 5 draft? MLB protection deadline is Nov. 17. The Rule 5 draft lets MLB teams take minor league players that other clubs have left off their 40-man rosters. A pick costs $100,000, and the new team must keep the player on its major league active roster all season or offer him back for $50,000. Clubs must decide whom to protect by 6 p.m. Eastern on Nov. 17, 2026.. MLB teams must set their 40-man rosters for Rule 5 protection by Nov. 17, 2026, ahead of a draft that a possible lockout could delay.. Eligibility depends on age and time in the system. A player who signed at 18 or younger becomes eligible before his fifth Rule 5 draft; one who signed at 19 or older, before his fourth. The rule exists so teams cannot hoard young players in the minors while other clubs would use them in the majors. Its name simply comes from its place, rule 5, in baseball's rulebook; the draft has been held every year since 1920. Some bargains became stars. The Pirates took Roberto Clemente from the Brooklyn Dodgers with the first pick in 1954, and Johan Santana, drafted in 1999, went on to win two Cy Young Awards with Minnesota. Josh Hamilton, Shane Victorino and Dan Uggla were also Rule 5 picks. The 2026 draft is scheduled for Dec. 9 at the Winter Meetings in San Diego, but it is in doubt. The labor deal expires Dec. 1, and in the 2021 lockout the major league phase was postponed while the minor league phase, which costs $24,000 per pick for Triple-A players, went ahead. The players' union has proposed moving this year's draft into November.

What is a consent decree? Meaning and recent DOJ cases. A consent decree is a court-approved settlement in which two parties resolve a dispute without either side admitting guilt or liability. The court keeps oversight of how the agreement is carried out. The term is most often used in the United States, and federal courts use it to enforce laws on antitrust, employment discrimination and environmental rules.. Harmeet Dhillon, the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division chief, resigned on Thursday after about 18 months in the post. Her tenure included dropping or ending several police and school consent decrees.. The arrangement is usually negotiated between a government body and an organization it has accused of wrongdoing. Once a judge signs it, the terms carry the force of a court order, and a violation can lead to further court action. Plaintiffs and defendants jointly ask the court to enter the agreement, and the court then supervises payments or changes in conduct. The term came up in the news this week when Harmeet Dhillon, assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, resigned on Thursday, according to Attorney General Todd Blanche. Under her leadership, the division dismissed more than 50 long-standing consent decrees with public school systems, many in the Deep South, that had protected Black students from unlawful discrimination. She also ended two pending decrees with the Minneapolis and Louisville police departments, which had followed investigations into systemic abuses, including in the wake of the killings of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor. Searchers also ask about consent decrees in several other settings. Police consent decrees are the most common in the news, and cities such as Chicago and Baltimore have operated under them after federal probes of their departments. For questions about a specific case, a lawyer is the appropriate contact.

What is a game-time decision? Meaning in the NFL injury report. What is a game-time decision? It is an injury status meaning a player's availability will not be settled until shortly before kickoff. In the NFL it is used when a team says a player may play or sit depending on how he feels that day, as the Jaguars said about running back Bhayshul Tuten for Thursday's game against the Ravens.. The Jacksonville Jaguars open Week 9 on Thursday Night Football against the Baltimore Ravens, and running back Bhayshul Tuten is listed as questionable with a foot and ankle injury, so his status will be decided close to kickoff.. Jacksonville's head coach, Liam Coen, said Tuten would be a game-time call for the Week 9 game in Baltimore. Tuten is listed as questionable, and he was absent from practice on Tuesday and Wednesday, even though Coen had expected him to take some part in practice. Under Coen, every player who did not practice during a week has missed that game, a pattern that points against Tuten playing. The label matters most for fantasy players and for the backup. If Tuten sits, Chris Rodriguez Jr., in his first season with Jacksonville, is expected to take a larger role. Teammate Travon Walker, a defensive end, is also questionable with a rib injury.

How does Alaska ranked choice voting work? Senate count on Nov. 18. In Alaska, voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no one wins more than 50% of first choices, the last-place candidate is dropped and those ballots move to each voter's next pick, round after round, until someone passes 50%. For the 2026 Senate race, that ranked-choice count is scheduled for Nov. 18.. Alaska's U.S. Senate race between Mary Peltola and Dan Sullivan was too close to call after the Nov. 3, 2026 vote, and is expected to be settled by the ranked-choice count on Nov. 18.. Alaska adopted the system by ballot measure in 2020 and kept it when voters narrowly rejected a repeal in 2024. It is used for the general election for governor, the state legislature, the U.S. House and the U.S. Senate. Before that, a single top-four primary sends the four leading candidates, of any party, to the November ballot. Voters may rank just one candidate or all four. The 2026 Senate ballot lists Democrat Mary Peltola, Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired Petersburg teacher listed with no party, and Republican Gerald L. Heikes. After election night neither leader had a majority: Peltola stood near 48% and led by roughly 600 votes. Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day are accepted for 10 days, and ballots from overseas for 15, so the count keeps moving. If no one passes 50% once all ballots are in, the state runs the ranked rounds on Nov. 18. Heikes and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. Would be eliminated first, and their few percent of the vote would flow to whichever candidate their voters ranked next. Ballots that ranked no one else simply drop out. With a margin this small, those transferred votes could decide the seat.
